EXP12B_TEXT: Each loop had one question, and it was the same question: the order of the new rows. After one new law, each adversary proved that no gap is left. In the two sets together, six agent-written law sets left the order of the new rows open, and the pilot's own laws in domain 2 left it open also. No law author read an order into the sentence "New entries go to the end of the file". The shipped code writes the new rows in starter order. A second implementation that follows the documentation can write them in a different order and satisfy each sentence.
SCALE_TEXT:
Each of the 24 blind runs gave the correct result on the first visit: a gap certificate when a law was absent, and a completeness proof when no law was absent. The largest task has 512 laws over 262,144 cases. Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 finished the two largest tasks in 67 s to 94 s. Haiku 5.5 needed 475 s and 814 s. One run cost $0.16 to $1.05.

The workers did not write these proofs by hand. Each worker wrote a small program that reads the laws, builds the decision tree again, and prints the Lean proof. For the 512-law tasks the proof files have 22 KB to 191 KB. The gate does not trust the program. It checks the proof.

This test did not find the size where the loop stops. For this family of rules, the number of laws is not the limit. The rules are simple: each law sets some inputs to constants. A domain with state, time or arithmetic needs a proof that a program cannot print from the laws. The one proof that the workers did not finish in this study is of that kind: the completeness proof for the lock, in two attempts by a weaker model (Section 9).
ABSTRACT_SCALE: A scale test with generated rules did not find the limit of the loop. With the laws in random order and no reference rule, adversaries gave the correct result in 24 of 24 runs, up to 512 laws over 262,144 cases, for $0.16 to $1.05 for one run. The folder path of each of these runs told the worker which kind of result was true, so a second set ran in neutral folders (Section 10). They wrote their own programs to build the proofs, and the gate checked the proofs. The one proof that the workers did not finish in this study is the completeness proof for the lock, in two attempts by a weaker model from a second vendor.
LIMIT_SCALE: The scale test of Section 8 reached 512 laws, but its rules are simple: each law sets inputs to constants. We did not measure where the loop stops for a domain with state, time or arithmetic.
VERIFY_TEXT: Our last run made 184 gate runs: 179 accept and 5 reject, and each verdict was the same as the run record. With the build caches present it took about 4 minutes with six parallel jobs. A first run builds each folder and takes longer.
ABSTRACT_BASELINE: A last test asks if the proof is necessary. A reviewer agent with no proof duty got the same question at {{BL_RUNS}} decision points of the study. It found {{BL_GAP_VALID}} of {{BL_GAP_TASKS}} gaps, at about the same cost and in less time. It missed one gap in {{BL_DUP_MISSED}} of {{BL_DUP_REVIEWS}} reviews, with two models, with and without tools: a legal input that a definition permits and its name does not suggest. The proof adversary found that gap at each of the three points. A wrong review had the same form as a correct review.

Revisions 4 and 5 have the full run of the proof pipeline on the real bugs and the audit of its conflict certificates (Section 12), the owner's decisions, the shipped fixes and the first proof on a product function (Section 13). Section 10 also corrects the blind set of Section 8: the first revision said that the adversary did not know which kind of result was true, and the folder path showed it.
PROOF_NEUTRAL_PARTIAL: We ran the Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 tasks of the blind set again, with the same brief, tools and gate, in folders with a hash for a name. 15 of 16 runs gave the correct result, and our gate accepted each with the extra kernels. In the last run (128 laws, Sonnet 5.5, a gap) the main kernel accepted the correct result two times. That proof is slow to check, about 18 minutes for one gate run, and the check with the extra kernels was not complete when this revision was written. The table of Section 8 shows the first runs. BUGS_PIPELINE_TEXT:
The proof pipeline on the same bugs (in work)

The proof pipeline has four workers for one bug. A model author writes a Lean mirror of the function, with a link test against the real function. A law author writes laws from the quoted documentation and has no view of the code. A prover gives a proof that the mirror passes the laws, or a conflict certificate: a proof that the code breaks one law on one legal input. The adversary gives a gap certificate or a completeness proof. The answer to each question is the result of the code after the fix. One tool does the checks for each function (tool/ in the archive). It replaces the gate scripts of the first study.

A pilot on five bugs is complete. It is not a score. It found two faults in our harness: a tool command that failed in a new folder, and a scoring rule that counted a function that the fix moved as a detection. The two are corrected, and one review detection and one data set record went out with the second. Three observations stand:

  • An agent can write the model. In five of five runs, the mirror agrees with the real function on 5,000 random cases, and the link test killed each generated mutant of the function (6 to 20 mutants).
  • A conflict certificate found a real bug. The docstring of one function says that it maps provider errors to the canonical failure classes. The prover showed that for HTTP status 404 the code returns a text that is not a class. That is the bug that the later fix removed.
  • A mirror of the code cannot show an omission. In one bug, the code ignored a field that it had to read. The mirror has no such field, the loop ended on a completeness proof, and the bug stayed hidden. Laws and types that are written from the documentation first do not have this limit.

The pipeline cost $3.49 to $5.95 for one bug, about ten times the cost of one review. The full run on the data set is the next step.
PROOF_NEUTRAL_NOTE: One run is not counted as correct (128 laws, Sonnet 5.5, a gap). The main kernel accepted its gap certificate two times, about 18 minutes for each gate run. Our gate run with the extra kernels ended with a reject after about 90 minutes. We found the probable cause later on a different proof: one of the extra kernels ends with a stack overflow on a deep proof term, and the comparator reports that as a reject (Section 13). We did not run the check of this proof again, because one of its kernel processes used more memory than the machine has.
